Maria Lopez: Quick heads-up — after the 2.3.0 kernel selector tweak we rolled yesterday, we see a consistent ~12-18% drop in prefix cache hit rate on private deployments vs hosted. Noticed in telemetry across two customers on VPC+NFS.
Ashok Patel: hmm. is this the kernel that prefers fused-attn for long sequence? could be a change in tokenization or key normalization. any sample IDs?
Maria Lopez: sample traces: req ids: r-1123, r-1145, r-1188. PerfResearch sent a small profile: cache_key normalized to raw prompt in private, but hashed prefix key in hosted.
PerfResearch: attaching quick snippet of the profiler output we ran:```
-- perf profile --
model: rwft-7b
seq: 2048
hosted: cache_hit_rate=0.72
private: cache_hit_rate=0.59
observed_path: key_generation -> serialize_kv -> netstore_write -> latency_spike
```
Jon Kim: If private is using netstore over NFS there's extra serialization + checksum we added for VPC durability. That can change timing and sometimes triggers a fallback in the runtime which changes KV key shape (we prefix with region+node-id on fallback).
Maria Lopez: exactly — found in logs: on Private we see `KV_FALLBACK=1` for many of the warmup requests, which causes prefix variant keys. Hosted sticks to in-memory/cache-local path.
Ashok Patel: Do we know why fallback triggers more on Private? config drift? kernel selection causing different batch shapes?
PerfResearch: Two causes from traces: (1) batch heuristic now prefers larger micro-batches on kernels with fused-attn which increases concurrent writes to netstore; (2) netstore client sees transient EIO on some NFS mounts and flips to fallback path. Both reduce hit-rate because of variant keying and delayed warmup propagation.
Maria Lopez: Repro steps I used: set model seq=2k, warmup prefix repeated 20x from same client, check `prefix-cache:stats` after 200 requests. Hosted shows hit-rate ~75% after 200 requests, Private ~58%.
Jon Kim: Proposed short fixes: 1) stop changing cache key shape on fallback (make key canonical and add metadata flags separately), 2) add jitter to netstore writes so we don't cause write storms with large micro-batches, 3) add better instrumentation for KV client to surface EIO->fallback rate.
Ashok Patel: +1 to canonical keys. If we don't change the logical key when we change transport, we can preserve hit surface. Might need a migration for on-disk / remote keys though.
PerfResearch: I ran a small experiment toggling `runtime.kv.canonical_keys=true` locally:```
# enable canonical keys
curl -X PATCH http://localhost:8080/_runtime/config -d '{"runtime.kv.canonical_keys": true}'
# re-run warmup script
./scripts/warmup_prefix.sh r-1123 20
```Result: private hit-rate moved to 68% (from 59%) in the same environment, latency tail unchanged.
infra-bot: deploy 2.3.1 candidate pushed to staging (build: infra/ci/2389).
Maria Lopez: nice. next action: roll canonical_keys to dedicated and a single private customer as canary, add netstore write jitter flag defaulted off for now. Also add tracepoint to capture `KV_KEY_SHAPE` and `KV_FALLBACK_REASON` on every write.
Jon Kim: I'll open a PR to: `runtime/kv: add canonical key mode` + `netstore: write_jitter_ms` + tracing fields. Will also add unit test asserting key canonicalization across transports.
Ashok Patel: can PerfResearch run the same experiment but with the kernel selector pinned to pre-2.3 (so we isolate batching vs netstore)?
PerfResearch: on it — I'll post numbers here in ~2 hours. initial guess: kernel change amplifies concurrent netstore writes which increases EIOs on some NFS configs -> fallback -> key divergence -> lower hit-rate.
Maria Lopez: thanks team. TL;DR: primary mitigation path = canonical keys + netstore jitter + better KV fallback telemetry. Can we get a small runbook note for support? put it under eng-runtime/playbooks/cache-warmup.md.
Jon Kim: will add runbook entry and PR link when ready.
PerfResearch: experiment update (short): with kernel pinned pre-2.3, private hit-rate was 71% (close to hosted). With kernel 2.3 and canonical_keys off it was 59%. With kernel 2.3 + canonical_keys on it was 69%. Seems kernel exposes the race but canonical keys recovers most of the loss.
Maria Lopez: perfect. I'll draft the customer note and schedule a canary deploy for canonical_keys. :thumbsup:
